body:
Why did the national movement enter a new phase after 1918?

The years from 1919 to 1922 marked an important change in the Indian national movement. Opposition to British rule increasingly involved students, workers, peasants, traders and other groups beyond the educated political leadership. Three connected developments explain this change: economic hardship after the First World War, anger against British repression, and Mahatma Gandhi's attempt to organise a nationwide non-violent struggle.

Economic and social distress after the war

The First World War (1914–1918) imposed heavy burdens on India. British military expenditure increased sharply, and the colonial government raised money through war loans and higher taxation. Customs duties increased, and income tax rates were increased during the war years.

Prices rose considerably. According to the NCERT account, prices approximately doubled between 1913 and 1918, making essential goods difficult to afford. Villages also faced pressure to supply soldiers. In some places, forced recruitment created resentment. Crop failures in 1918–1919 and 1920–1921, together with an influenza epidemic, caused further suffering.

Many Indians expected conditions to improve after the war ended. Instead, the continuation of restrictive colonial policies increased dissatisfaction. The government appeared willing to demand sacrifices from Indians without granting them corresponding political freedoms.

Gandhi's approach to political struggle

Mahatma Gandhi returned to India in January 1915 after organising campaigns against racial discrimination in South Africa. He brought with him the method of satyagraha, which relied on truth, non-violence and the willingness to suffer rather than inflict suffering on an opponent.

Satyagraha

Satyagraha means holding firmly to truth. In Gandhian political practice, it involved resisting injustice through non-violent action, moral persuasion and self-discipline. It was an active method of resistance, not simply the absence of action.

Gandhi tested this approach in local Indian struggles before launching a nationwide campaign. In Champaran, Bihar, in 1917, he supported indigo cultivators suffering under the plantation system. In Ahmedabad, Gujarat, in 1918, he intervened in a dispute involving textile mill workers. In Kheda, Gujarat, in 1918, he supported peasants seeking relief from land revenue demands following crop failure.

These campaigns established an important connection between local grievances and political action. Peasants could organise around revenue demands, workers around employment conditions, and wider sections of society around restrictions on civil liberties. Gandhi believed that such struggles could be united through disciplined non-violent action.

The immediate political turning point

In 1919 the British government introduced legislation giving the authorities extraordinary powers against suspected political opponents. Gandhi called for a nationwide hartal on 6 April 1919 to oppose it. A hartal is a collective stoppage of ordinary activity, often involving the closure of shops and workplaces as a form of protest.

The response showed that opposition to British rule could spread across different towns and communities. It also exposed a major difficulty: maintaining non-violence during a large movement when public anger and official repression were increasing.

Prelims focus

  • The First World War lasted from 1914 to 1918.
  • Gandhi returned to India in January 1915.
  • Champaran Satyagraha was associated with Bihar and indigo cultivators in 1917.
  • Ahmedabad mill workers and Kheda peasants were associated with Gandhian struggles in Gujarat in 1918.
  • The nationwide anti-Rowlatt hartal was called for 6 April 1919.
  • Trap: Satyagraha was an active form of non-violent resistance, not armed rebellion or passive acceptance of injustice.

[Sources: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World—II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed pp. 54–55; NCERT, Our Pasts—III, Class 8, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 115–116; Mani Bhavan Gandhi Sangrahalaya, Satyagrahas of Mahatma Gandhi, chronology entries for 1917–1919, consulted 21 November 2026.]

title: India after the First World War: The Background to Mass Nationalism

body:
What was the Rowlatt Act?

The Rowlatt Act of 1919, formally known as the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, 1919, extended extraordinary powers to the colonial government for dealing with suspected revolutionary and political activities. It was associated with the recommendations of a committee chaired by Justice Sidney Rowlatt.

The legislation was passed by the Imperial Legislative Council despite strong opposition from its Indian members. It permitted severe restrictions on political activity and allowed the authorities to detain suspected political prisoners without trial for up to 2 years.

Indian nationalists considered the law especially objectionable because it restricted basic liberties even after the First World War had ended. The government claimed that extraordinary security powers were necessary; nationalists argued that such powers could be used to suppress legitimate political opposition.

Why the law was opposed

Detention without trial means holding a person in custody without first establishing guilt through an ordinary criminal trial. The objection to the Rowlatt Act was therefore not merely that punishment was severe. It was that the government could restrict personal liberty without the normal safeguards of a trial.

Nationalists also called the legislation the Black Act. This was a critical nickname, not its formal legal title.

The Rowlatt Satyagraha

Gandhi proposed non-violent civil disobedience against the unjust legislation. The campaign called upon people to protest peacefully through public meetings, prayers, processions and hartals.

A nationwide hartal was organised on 6 April 1919. Shops closed in several towns, workers stopped work, and public demonstrations took place. Although the agitation extended across India, its strongest organisational presence was in cities and towns. It had not yet brought rural India into sustained political action on the scale later seen during Non-Cooperation.

Why did the situation become tense in Punjab?

Punjab experienced particularly intense protests. In Amritsar, Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr Satyapal were important local leaders opposing the legislation. Their arrest and removal from the city provoked widespread anger.

On 10 April 1919, police fired upon a procession in Amritsar. The confrontation was followed by attacks on government-linked buildings and violence in the city. British authorities imposed harsh restrictions and deployed military forces.

The crisis reached a devastating point on 13 April 1919, when troops fired on a gathering at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar.

Suspension of the campaign

Gandhi had insisted that a satyagraha must remain non-violent. As protests and official repression were followed by violent incidents in several places, he concluded that participants were not sufficiently prepared to maintain the required discipline.

He suspended the Rowlatt Satyagraha in April 1919. This decision did not mean that the Rowlatt Act had become acceptable. It reflected Gandhi's belief that a movement based on non-violence should not continue through uncontrolled violence.

Prelims focus

  • The Rowlatt Act was enacted in 1919.
  • Its formal name was the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, 1919.
  • It was associated with Justice Sidney Rowlatt.
  • It allowed detention of suspected political prisoners without trial for up to 2 years.
  • Gandhi called a nationwide hartal for 6 April 1919.
  • Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr Satyapal were associated with anti-Rowlatt agitation in Amritsar.
  • Trap: Gandhi suspended the Rowlatt Satyagraha in April 1919; the Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn later, in February 1922.

[Sources: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World—II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed pp. 55–56; NCERT, Our Pasts—III, Class 8, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed p. 116; NCERT, Social and Political Life—III, Class 8, chapter Understanding Laws, Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh sidebar, printed p. 44, 2018–19 edition; Press Information Bureau, Government of India, account of Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew and the Rowlatt agitation, consulted 21 November 2026; Mani Bhavan Gandhi Sangrahalaya, Detailed Chronology, entries for April 1919, consulted 21 November 2026.]

title: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 and Gandhi's Nationwide Satyagraha

body:
What happened at Jallianwala Bagh?

On 13 April 1919, the day of the Baisakhi festival, a large gathering assembled at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, Punjab. Some people had come to participate in or support political protests; others were visitors who had come to the city for the festival. Many were unaware of the restrictions imposed by the authorities.

Jallianwala Bagh was an enclosed open ground surrounded by walls and buildings, with limited means of exit. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer arrived with troops and ordered them to fire on the crowd without warning. The confined setting made escape extremely difficult.

The firing killed and injured large numbers of unarmed civilians. The contemporary official death toll was 379, with approximately 1,200 reported wounded. The actual number of deaths remains disputed, and other estimates are higher. It is therefore important to identify the official count as an official figure rather than present it as the unquestioned final total.

Who were Dyer and O'Dwyer?

Two British officials with similar surnames are frequently confused in accounts of the massacre.

  • Reginald Dyer: The military officer who commanded the troops and ordered firing at Jallianwala Bagh on 13 April 1919.
  • Michael O'Dwyer: The Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab at the time. He was responsible for the provincial administration and subsequently defended Dyer's action.

The distinction is between the military commander who gave the immediate order to fire and the provincial administrator who supported the action. They were not the same person.

Repression and reactions

The massacre occurred during a wider period of repression in Punjab. Restrictions on movement, public humiliation, corporal punishment and other harsh measures intensified anger against colonial rule. The episode demonstrated how far the authorities were prepared to go in suppressing political opposition.

Rabindranath Tagore renounced his British knighthood in protest against the atrocities. His decision gave prominent public expression to the anger and grief felt across India.

The massacre also changed the political atmosphere. For many Indians, it seriously damaged confidence that the British government would safeguard civil liberties or respond fairly to constitutional protest. Opposition to the Rowlatt Act became part of a wider moral and political challenge to colonial rule.

The historical connection

The Rowlatt Act was a repressive law. The Rowlatt Satyagraha was the movement organised against it. The Jallianwala Bagh massacre was an atrocity committed during the repression surrounding that agitation. These are connected events, but they are not interchangeable names for a single event.

Why did it matter for later movements?

When Gandhi and the Congress subsequently proposed Non-Cooperation, they referred to the injustice committed in Punjab as one of the major reasons Indians should withdraw support from the colonial government. The massacre therefore contributed directly to the political atmosphere in which the Non-Cooperation Movement emerged.

Prelims focus

  • Jallianwala Bagh massacre: 13 April 1919.
  • Location: Amritsar, Punjab.
  • The event occurred on Baisakhi.
  • Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer ordered the firing.
  • The contemporary official death toll was 379; the actual total is disputed.
  • Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood in protest.
  • Trap: Reginald Dyer was the military commander; Michael O'Dwyer was the Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab.

[Sources: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World—II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed p. 56; NCERT, Our Pasts—III, Class 8, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed p. 116; National Army Museum, London, Online Collection, Native crawling up street where Miss Sherwood was assaulted, 1919, accession 1972-05-81-4-1, historical description and casualty figures, consulted 21 November 2026; National Portrait Gallery, London, Sir Michael Francis O'Dwyer, biographical entry, consulted 21 November 2026.]

title: Jallianwala Bagh: The Massacre of 13 April 1919 and Its Political Impact

body:
What was the Khilafat issue?

The Khilafat Movement developed among Indian Muslims after the First World War. The war ended with the defeat of the Ottoman Empire, whose ruler had also claimed the position of Caliph or Khalifa.

Caliph and Khilafat

The Caliph was regarded by many Muslims as a leader representing the wider Islamic community. Khilafat refers to the institution or authority of the Caliph. In this movement, Indian Muslim leaders were particularly concerned about the Ottoman Caliph's position, his political authority and the status of Muslim sacred places after the war.

Indian Muslim leaders feared that the victorious powers would impose a harsh peace settlement on the Ottoman ruler. They demanded that the Caliph retain sufficient authority and that Muslim sacred places remain protected. This was an issue arising from developments outside India, but it generated strong political mobilisation within India.

Organisation and leadership

A Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919. Important leaders included the brothers Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali, commonly called the Ali brothers.

They sought public support against the proposed treatment of the Ottoman Caliph. The movement involved meetings, petitions, political organisation and eventually cooperation with Gandhi's campaign against British rule.

Why did Gandhi support the Khilafat Movement?

Gandhi believed that a successful nationwide struggle against colonial rule required cooperation between Hindus and Muslims. Supporting the Khilafat cause offered an opportunity to bring Muslim political mobilisation into a common anti-colonial campaign.

The alliance brought together 3 related but distinct demands:

  • Redress of the Punjab wrongs: A response to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the repression of 1919.
  • Redress of the Khilafat wrong: Opposition to the harsh treatment of the Ottoman Caliph and threats to his position.
  • Swaraj: The demand that Indians gain self-government instead of remaining subject to colonial rule.

Swaraj means self-rule. In the context of Non-Cooperation, it expressed the objective of ending political dependence on British authority. The Khilafat demand, by contrast, was specifically concerned with the position of the Ottoman Caliph. The two causes were politically linked without being identical.

From separate grievances to common action

Gandhi discussed united action with Khilafat leaders and travelled with Shaukat Ali to mobilise public support. At the special Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress in September 1920, Gandhi argued for a Non-Cooperation Movement supporting both the Khilafat cause and the demand for swaraj.

This combination helped widen participation. Many Muslims joined a movement that was simultaneously concerned with an international religious-political issue and India's colonial subordination. Many Hindu nationalists supported the common programme as part of the struggle for self-rule.

The importance and limitations of the alliance

The Khilafat–Non-Cooperation alliance created an important period of Hindu–Muslim political cooperation. It broadened the social reach of the Congress-led movement and gave local Khilafat organisations a role in nationwide mobilisation.

However, the alliance did not mean that every participant understood swaraj in the same way, or that religious and political differences permanently disappeared. Its immediate strength came from cooperation around shared action against British policies.

Prelims focus

  • The Khilafat issue arose after the Ottoman Empire's defeat in the First World War.
  • The Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919.
  • Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali were prominent Khilafat leaders.
  • Gandhi supported the movement as a means of strengthening Hindu–Muslim cooperation.
  • The common campaign linked the Punjab wrongs, the Khilafat wrong and the demand for swaraj.
  • The Congress special session at Calcutta in September 1920 supported the proposed Non-Cooperation Movement.
  • Trap: The Khilafat demand concerned the Ottoman Caliph; swaraj concerned self-government in India.

[Sources: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World—II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed pp. 56–57; NCERT, Our Pasts—III, Class 8, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed p. 117; NCERT, Themes in Indian History—Part III, Class 12, chapter Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, Khilafat Movement explanatory box, printed p. 350; Indian National Congress, Synopsis of Plenary Sessions from 1885 to 2018, Special Session Calcutta, 1920, consulted 21 November 2026.]

title: The Khilafat Movement and the Formation of the Hindu–Muslim Political Alliance
